lesson.title: The While Loop: Repeating Until Something Changes
lesson.summary: A while loop repeats a block of code for as long as a boolean condition stays True, making it the right tool when you don't know ahead of time how many repetitions you'll need.
lesson.body:
Where a for loop is driven by a sequence of items, a while loop is driven by a boolean expression, the same kind of True-or-False test you already use in if statements. A while loop keeps repeating its body as long as that condition evaluates to True, and it stops the moment the condition evaluates to False. This makes it the right choice whenever you cannot know in advance how many times you'll need to repeat, only what the stopping condition should eventually look like.

The syntax is simple: the keyword while, a boolean expression, a colon, and an indented body, just like the header of an if statement, except the block underneath can run more than once. Before every single pass through the body, Python re-evaluates that condition completely from scratch. If it is True, the body runs again; if it is False, the loop ends immediately and execution continues with whatever comes after it.

Consider this example:
count = 1
while count <= 3:
    print(count, "Mississippi")
    count += 1
Trace it carefully, because while loops require you to track state across passes rather than relying on a sequence to run out. Before the first pass, count is 1, and 1 <= 3 is True, so the body runs: it prints "1 Mississippi" and then count becomes 2. Before the second pass, 2 <= 3 is True, so it prints "2 Mississippi" and count becomes 3. Before the third pass, 3 <= 3 is still True, so it prints "3 Mississippi" and count becomes 4. Before the fourth pass, 4 <= 3 is False, so the loop stops without running its body a fourth time.

Notice that count += 1 is doing essential work here: it is exactly what eventually makes the condition False. If that line were missing, count would stay at 1 forever, the condition 1 <= 3 would never stop being True, and the program would loop endlessly, a situation covered in detail as infinite loops. Every well-formed while loop you write needs some line in its body that moves the tracked state closer to making the condition false, or the loop has no way to ever finish.

While loops shine in situations a for loop cannot handle cleanly, especially input validation, where the number of attempts truly cannot be known in advance because it depends entirely on what the user actually types:
password = input("Enter password: ")
while password != "secret":
    password = input("Try again: ")
This keeps asking for input for as many tries as it takes, stopping only once the condition password != "secret" finally becomes False, whether that happens on the first attempt or the fiftieth. A for loop simply has no clean way to express this, because there is no sequence to iterate over in advance, only a condition that gets tested repeatedly against whatever the user types next.

This also explains why the Boolean Expressions concept matters so much here: everything a while loop can do is limited by how precisely you can phrase its condition. Comparisons like <=, ==, and !=, along with combinations built from and, or, and not, are exactly the vocabulary a while loop's header speaks, so getting comfortable writing accurate boolean expressions pays off directly in writing correct while loops.
